extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media critics, and informed readers interested in media bias and news quality
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and normative criteria for journalistic practice and news coverage, drawing on Chomsky's 'propaganda model', framing/agenda-setting theory, and contemporary critiques of media economics and polarization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the journalist in a liberal democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of the journalist in a liberal democracy as watchdog, provider of information necessary for informed debate, and as a voice of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should serve these democratic functions despite pressures not to challenge accepted narratives; failing to do so undermines informed debate and civic voice. The piece notes internal pressures (fear of breaking rank) and external pressures that discourage challenging narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as reconstruction / selective representation
rubrics_metrics.description: “News is not an exact representation of reality but rather a reconstruction from various angles of a small section of reality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implies that coverage is inherently selective; journalists do not necessarily lie or consciously distort, but by choosing particular stories, sources, and angles they construct a version of reality. Awareness of this selectivity is a criterion for assessing news reliability and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing
rubrics_metrics.description: “The frame is the overarching angle of how the various stories are treated once they are covered.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing influences how a story is investigated and reported, who is interviewed, what questions are asked, and how information is interpreted. Framing is described as inherently ideological (whether conscious or not); good reporting should recognize and, where appropriate, challenge limiting frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda setting / Gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: “While agenda setting or gatekeeping decides what a newspaper or broadcaster covers or does not cover…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about what to cover (and what to omit) shape public debate; evaluating news requires scrutiny of what topics are regularly excluded or deprioritized and why (e.g., service to particular interests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 1 — Ownership and profit orientation of the media
rubrics_metrics.description: Mainstream outlets are typically large corporations or part of large conglomerates and the information presented will be biased toward those interests; news items that challenge these interests or endanger them will be censored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether coverage aligns with the economic or political interests of owners/conglomerates; presence of systematic omission or soft treatment of topics harming owner interests is evidence of this filter at work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 2 — Funding sources, namely advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: The news is “filler” to get readers to see the ads; news that conflicts with the interests of advertisers will be marginalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editorial decisions for deference to advertisers' interests, patterns of marginalizing stories that might reduce ad revenue, and whether news is treated primarily as a vehicle for commercial messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 3 — Sourcing mass-media news
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters depend on official sources of information, and if they question these, they may be denied access; reporters shy away from writing articles that will offend or harm these official sources—corporate, government, or expert—for fear of losing access; as a result, reporters adopt an uncritical stance and in doing so can avoid experiencing cognitive dissonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reliance on official sources, the balance of source types (official vs independent/critical), and whether access concerns lead to uncritical reporting. Anti-pattern: unquestioning repetition of official narratives because of fear of losing access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 4 — Flak and the enforcers
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reporter casts doubt on a prevailing narrative that favours established power, they or the organization they work for will get 'flak' and be discredited; it’s a way of disciplining the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for organized campaigns, legal threats, or reputational attacks used to punish or silence dissenting reporting. The ability to produce 'flak' is tied to power; presence of flak shapes editorial caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 5 — Fear ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally 'anti-communism' in the Cold War context, updated to 'fear' — when any fear-based fervor is aroused it has a dual purpose: partly to get rid of people you don’t like, partly to frighten the rest so they will accept authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how fear narratives or moral panics narrow acceptable debate, exclude certain topics or actors, and are mobilized in ways useful to elite interests. Watch for fear-driven framing that stifles dissent or critical investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge accepted narratives / willingness to contradict mainstream lines
rubrics_metrics.description: It can be difficult for reporters to challenge accepted narratives and not be marginalized in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good journalism requires willingness to investigate counter-narratives (example: marine biologist Boris Worm contradicting mainstream seal/cod story), find and present contrary evidence, and persist despite marginalization. Anti-pattern: abandoning investigation because a story is already 'established.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide complexity and context rather than simplistic equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid boiling complex systems down to one simple mathematical equation (e.g., 'less seals equal more cod'); when a story gets planted and continually reinforced it may be treated as fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reporting for depth: does it explore ecological, economic, or historical complexity and multiple causal factors? Good reporting challenges reductive narratives and explains interrelated causes (e.g., overfishing, altered ecosystem states, political motives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust reporters but scrutinize institutional context
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Most journalists work for giant nihilistic corporations whose editorial decisions are skewed by a toxic mix of political and financial considerations.’ Nevertheless, Taibbi insists people should trust reporters while noting the problematic context they operate in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both individual reporting quality and the institutional/editorial constraints shaping coverage. Distinguish between reporter integrity and systemic pressures that bias editorial choices; support and protect reporters who pursue critical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware manufactured dissent and divisive framing that obscures larger problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The press has increasingly used intramural hatreds to obscure larger, more damning truths; 'fake controversies' have been deployed to keep audiences from seeing larger problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether coverage amplifies contrived controversies or polarizing disputes that distract from systemic issues. Good journalism should expose when dissent is manufactured to divide audiences and should reframe to surface underlying systemic causes.
